  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Vignette:
# Luca Rossi

Luca Rossi was thirty-two when the warehouse fire trapped him on the second floor. He had worked at Brennan Logistics for eight years, moving steadily from dock associate to supervisor—reliable, punctual, the kind of man his wife Maria called steady. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, a faulty electrical panel ignited in the storage section where Luca was conducting inventory. The alarm system failed. What he remembers now, with a clarity that exhausts him, is not the full sequence of events but a series of vivid, isolated moments: the smell of accelerant and burning plastic suddenly overwhelming; the sight of a coworker, Derek, deliberately kicking over a stack of pallets to clear an escape route, leaving two junior employees scrambling behind him; the texture of the rough concrete wall he pressed his palms against, searching for a door in the black smoke, feeling that grit embed itself into his skin. Luca made it out through a side window. Derek did not wait for anyone. Two people died in the stairwell.

In the months that followed, Luca told himself the story differently. He had been lucky. The fire was not as bad as the news made it sound. Derek had panicked like anyone would. But these retellings never quite stuck. The moments remained—snapshots, each one sharper than any ordinary memory. When he tried to think of his daughter's sixth birthday party the previous month, the details were soft, almost watercolor. But the texture of that concrete, Derek's face as he kicked the pallets aside, the sound of the alarm that didn't work—these arrived in his mind with the force of something still happening.

What frightened Luca most was not the fire itself but what it meant about people. Derek's choice to save himself, to actively prevent others from following, had fractured something in Luca's sense of safety. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally selfish, that proximity to others was proximity to potential abandonment or harm. When he returned to the retail position he had taken after leaving Brennan—a more modest role, but one that kept him away from warehouse work—he found himself hyperaware of his coworkers' small transgressions. A colleague who cut in front of him at the time clock, a manager who didn't acknowledge his greeting, a customer who was rude to another employee—each of these felt like evidence of moral collapse, proof that the world was full of people like Derek. His vigilance became exhausting. Colleagues began to notice that Luca seemed distant, occasionally hostile to minor infractions that would normally go unremarked.

The shame came when he allowed himself to remember fully. He had not helped the two who died. He had saved himself. Was he different from Derek, or simply luckier in where he had been standing? This question lived in his chest, and when it surfaced, the shame was so intense that he had learned to suppress it through sheer force of will—pushing the memories down, refusing to think about the event, telling himself it hadn't been that bad. But suppression required energy he didn't have, and lately he had begun to hurt himself in small ways to interrupt the thoughts: pressing his thumbnail hard into his palm, holding ice until his fingers burned, anything to replace the internal noise with something sharp and external and controllable.

Maria had noticed the marks on his hands. She had asked about his withdrawal, his silences at dinner. Three weeks ago, when she found him in the garage pressing a lighter to his forearm, she insisted he see someone. Luca came to his first appointment reluctant, convinced that talking would only make the memories more real, more present. But the vivid snapshots were already there, and they were not going away.
